Had to break it into two parts:

Part 1 -

First off, if you ever have sucidal thoughts, PLEASE reach out to your local suicide hotline. In the USA it's: 800-273-8255. Just know: you have a purpose to be here. You matter. Your life matters. You are healing and growing and your story can help others heal and grow. Don't forget how valuable your life is. 

Second, PLEASE STOP COUNTING CALORIES AND PLEASE ALLOW YOURSELF TO EAT. No matter what you have eaten throughout the day or day before or how much you exercise, you are allowed to eat!! When I was counting calories to loose weight, my Dr. told me the amount that my app was telling me to eat was the very baseline for my body to exist for 1 day. No thinking, no moving, no other energy expulsion. Living takes calories and those apps are super unhealthy for you, especially at your age! Please ditch the apps and calorie counting. Also, I highly recommend you stop weighing yourself, body checking, overexercising etc. This can seem like a lot of behaviors to shift at once so be patient with yourself, but know that you CAN change!

Third, be proud of yourself for reaching out and being able to talk about these intense experiences and your struggles. Both are HUGE steps towards healing so congrats on this first big step!

Fourth, Here we go, my apologies for the insanely long response but I hope it's helpful!

I would highly recommend seeing a therapist or counselor. It sounds like you have experienced repeated severe trauma that is and will continue to be the root cause of your disordered eating. Do not blame yourself or feel that you are broken. Your disordered eating was protecting you against the pain and trauma that you were experiencing. It was/is a coping mechanism, a protective force in your life. But it is not serving your full best interest so it's time to learn to find new coping mechanisms and ways to heal. The healing and recovery process is difficult, non-linear (meaning ups and downs), but TOTALLY worth it. You're young and already on the right path by reaching out and having self awareness. You're doing great! However, to further your healing process, I’d highly recommend seeking help from an ED-specializing therapist who practices the health at every size (HAES) and intuitive eating approach. You can search for providers on the [HAES](https://haescommunity.com/) website or search your town, the type of provider, and "intuitive eating or health at every size" in Google. With COVID, lots of therapists are doing virtual sessions so you don't necessarily need someone local. I'd look into HAES and intuitive eating yourself (there are many books, podcasts, instagram accounts, etc. devoted to these. See my below list for some starters). As another commenter mentioned, it's probably extreme hunger, if you're recovering from a restrictive ED, and it's totally normal. I experienced it a lot in the first few weeks/months of my most successful recovery that gave me the ability to eat intuitively and without guilt for almost 2 full years. Your body needs to learn to trust you again. Just remember that what you're experiencing IS recovery and it's totally okay considering what your body's been through :)

Hi, 

I work as a counselor for people who struggle with eating disorders. I don't know how old you are, but I want you to know this is a very dangerous path to go down. Eating disorders absolutely suck the life out of beautiful intelligent vibrant young people. 

The way you already associate eating with guilt is very unhealthy. I would talk to your parents if you trust them, if you don't, talk to your PCP or school counselor. You need to help yourself now before things get worse. Guilt from eating isn't normal, and recognizing that is first coping step. Second is reaching out for help, you owe it to yourself. Third coping step is honestly sitting with those guilty/uncomfortable thoughts. Training yourself to sit through uncomfortable thoughts and not acting on them/letting them get to you is a valuable life skill. Just because you are feeling guilty, doesn't mean you should or that you deserve it. 

Everyone deserves to eat regardless of who they are or what they've done. It's a basic human right. 

Please seek help now. What you're going through is not fun and it's not a shameful thing to ask for help. Especially if you are young, eating disorders sometimes can follow you for life if you don't seek proper treatment. 

Recovery is so possible. It's can be long and sometimes not linear. Be patient with yourself! ❤️

text:
My guess is you're still attempting to restrict these foods, labeling them as "bad", or only allowing yourself to have a certain amount per day. What you're effectively doing is placing these foods on a pedestal and making them "special." Humans are not that complex - if you make something "special", that thing will become highly desirable. Think of the kids you knew from your childhood who were only allowed limited TV time at home. Weren't they the most TV-obsessed kids you've ever met? Your trigger foods are your TV.   
  
A big thing for me in recovery was giving myself unconditional permission to eat all foods. Of course, this didn't mean that a switch flipped in my brain and I immediately stopped overeating my trigger foods. At first, there were definitely nights when I intended to stop at just one bowl of ice cream but ended up eating the whole pint. But, let me tell you, after a consecutive week of consuming a pint of ice cream every night, ice cream actually becomes pretty boring and unremarkable. You may even discover that you don't like it all that much and would prefer to eat other things.   
  
This is literally what happened to me in recovery. When I was ill and starved and restricting I was OBSESSED with ice cream. I absolutely could not have it in the house. If I had a pint in my freezer, that pint of ice cream would consume my thoughts all day long (it was exhausting!) until eventually I would binge on it that same day. Now that it's just another food that I'm allowed to have whenever I want (and not a "special" food) I've realized that it's actually not my preference. It's never my dessert of choice when eating out and I don't really put it in my shopping cart at the store anymore. If my partner buys it, I may have a scoop, but for the most part I forget that it's even in the freezer. I truly prefer eating other things /find other foods more enjoyable!!! Who knew!??!!?  
  
All this to say, I don't know all the details of your particular ED, but I'm willing to bet that your so-called "lack of self-control" is not really a thing. It's scary to tell yourself that you are allowed all foods - and to actually follow through with it. It feels like you're letting go of "control". But the thing that you need to realize is that putting these foods on a pedestal actually gives them control over you - and you need to take that power back. Good luck to you - you've got this!

text:
I recommend looking up inuitive eating! The biggest help to me was eating regular meals throughout the day- starting first thing in the morning with a big breakfast. 

A principle of inuitive eating is honoring your hunger and eating what your body is wanting. Another principle is also listening to your body and how it feels after you eat. Your doctor is probably saying the first part but not the second. 

Often after binges or eating a large amount of carbs/sugar, our bodies feel heavy and lethargic. We can even vomit from eating too much. Eventually, you can start to make the connection of eating certain foods/eating too much makes you feel awful and you start to adjust what you are eating because you want to feel good after eating. 

You may even eat a bunch of carbs/sugars in the beginning and that's totally fine. You just have to give it time and trust the process. Eventually you will get tired of how you feel, make that connection, and then start making different choices. For me, my cravings went from sugar to carbs to protein to fruit to vegetables. Some weeks I eat more carbs and no fruits or vegetables. Some weeks I can only handle eating fruits OR vegetables but not both. Im listening to my body and that's what's important.

Another important principle is recognizing the different types of hunger- we eat socially, we eat to deal with feelings, and we eat to deal with physical hunger. Recognizing what type of hunger you have helps you base your choices on eating vs using a different coping skill. For social settings, you still need to eat (aka dont save all your eating for the day at the party) throughout the day, but instead of having a full meal before the party, you might just have a snack instead.

text: In my multifamily therapy sessions, supports are coached to speak from their experience and express their emotions authentically. Use I feel statements to communicate how your loved one's behavior is impacting you. You might say something like, "When you spend so much time and energy planning new diets, I feel like there is more distance between us and that hurts me." Or "I've noticed that you've been looking at diet ideas that seem unhealthy and unsustainable. That makes me feel very worried about your wellbeing because I love you and want you to be well." Then ask directly how they feel about it and if they are willing to talk about ideas for getting professional help. You're right that you cannot force someone to seek help or get better. I think that it can be really important to provide an outsiders perspective on the behaviors though. EDs are very sneaky especially when the behavior begins early on. You don't necessarily notice how much of an impact it's having on your relationships and daily functioning until someone points it out. Or they might know that they're relapsing and feel helpless to stop it. It's impossible to say where they're at, so ask directly and be prepared to receive answers that may surprise you or not make much sense in your brain. Eating disorders are mental illnesses and the reasoning of a sick brain doesn't make any logical sense. Try to remain non judgemental about the behaviors and not engage with ED logic very much. It's important to let them express how they feel about this even if you know it's logically or factually wrong. Have the mindset of wanting to understand what's happening in their head and their life that's driving the behaviors rather than trying to argue or shame them into realizing that her beliefs about her weight or food are wrong. I would be prepared that this conversation may make them upset. You could do everything right and they may still get angry and defensive. EDs often function as a way to make someone feel safe and in control. When you notice the behaviors, that can make the person feel like you're trying to take away their ability to feel safe. Choose a calm, quiet environment to start the conversation. Avoid initiating it at a meal or directly before/after.

1) Try to eat some red lentils- they are such a great healthy food too. Here’s how I cook mine: be sure and rinse them not to only clean them but also to get extra starch and stuff off so they cook nice and fluffy. I do 2 cups of water mixed with better than boullion vegetable flavor to taste mix that up and then add 1 cup of red lentils (so a 2:1 ratio). You will boil it together so I usually gently stir it until it starts to boil and once it comes to a boil I turn the heat down and put a lid on it in a way it can vent. Then you simmer it until the water basically boils out- they cook quick so maybe 30-40 ish minutes?  After it’s done often I’ll add a can of diced/stewed tomatoes and a can of either chick peas or whatever bean I have on tap. Any of the white beans go well or kidney beans. And voila. This is pretty much the meal that helped me recover and I still eat it very often because it’s easy and keeps well to take to work and heat up. You should have no problem pooing as there is enough fiber in that to probably knit a pair of socks.

One thing to keep in mind is that red lentils don’t do well in stuff like an instant pot they are too fragile and get hella mushy. Could sub green or black lentils if you want to do instant pot.

2) Another great way to add fiber and protein is also to make pasta, use whatever flavor of tomato sauce you like and the when the pasta is almost finished cooking throw in some beans to that before you drain and add the sauce. Again white beans like cannellini work great as do kidney beans. This stated out as a poor in college “struggle meal” but it’s a great easy way to some fiber and protein to a low energy cooking day too.

3) You can also buy flavored water packets with fiber that are pretty cheap and despite the sound they are actually good and appealing!

4) Get a bag of little cutie or any variety of those tiny bagged mandarin oranges and eat a couple through out the day. 

5) Be sure you are drinking enough water too! Water is reabsorbed in the large intestine and your body generally will absorb more to preserve water if you are dehydrated.

text:
For me, I had to stop the purges before the binges. There was something about purging that really impacted my view of myself, and I would feel disgusting and worthless after - so cue a few hours later or the next day, I would binge as a way to almost make myself feel whole again. Plus, its been shown that purging affects your ability to self-regulate appetite, and since I was filling my body with binge-type foods (nutritionally poor to begin with) and then purging that out, my body was also naturally starving for nutrition so I was genuinely hungry all the time, and would lead to binges. Binge-eating is a serious eating disorder, but it becomes so much worse when paired with bulimia. 

It's hard enough to fix one, so I would suggest trying to resist the urge to purge, and just hold whatever you eat down even if you feel like shit because of it. If you've already gotten to that stage and you're still binging, try shifting your mentality - rather than making yourself feel guilty and horrible and punishing yourself when you binge, allow yourself these foods without caveats or strings attached (ie I'll just have one bite or limit myself to half). I found that once I let myself have whatever my brain was demanding, even if it was a "binge food", I stopped craving those things so intensely, and stopped reaching for them in comfort because they no longer felt like indulgent forbidden foods. For example, I genuinely am not that into candy or candy bars (would much rather hit my sweet tooth with a high quality dessert), but I would buy these as part of my binge sessions because they were things that my brain deemed as forbidden foods. Instead, I went for what I actually love as an indulgent food; a brownie with strawberries for example. And for some reason, because I was genuinely enjoying it, I felt more satisfied and less of that bottomless need to continue consuming until I was disgusted with myself.

I know this is the same stuff you've heard before but eventually you've got to just try and view the food you're binging on differently. Your body / brain becomes accustomed to this perverse, harmful rewarding / punishing feeling when you binge - remove how you view the food and that feeling stops being so present when you do eat, and as a result your eating habits will slowly begin to normalize.

Just my experience!

text:
It's a really tricky one because it's different for everyone. Firstly just want to say that you're doing really well already- so many people jump into the angry/defensive/confrontational approach, or start making assumptions about what's going on in people with EDs brains, which really doesn't help at all. Generally just being there for her is the most important thing that you can do.

Other than that, ask questions (though definitely try to avoid talking about anything ED related over meals unless she initiates the conversation). She's not likely to be annoyed at you for asking how you can support her. She might not have an answer yet, but it opens up the conversation, shows that you're willing to help and (if she's not already) gets her thinking about what support might actually be beneficial. E.g. some people find it helpful to have a meal plan, to have someone sit with them after meals, or to have only a few days worth of food in the cupboard. Personally, when I feel like purging the most helpful thing is just being able to curl up next to my fiance (feels kind of like a safe space to me where I can focus on being warm and cosy), so we have a sort of unspoken deal that if I tell him I'm having a bad day he'll deal with me invading his personal space and cuddle me for an hour or so while we watch a film or something. In contrast, other people might need some time alone to just sit and deal with the anxiety, so it's really important to ask! On a side note, "feeling sick" can be a gentler way of saying fullness related anxiety, but that could be different for her.

I guess some good starting questions to help you understand would be: Does she know what's triggered the relapse? What would help prevent it happening (or reduce the frequency of it happening) in future? And would she like you to take an active role in her recovery, or simply just be there for support while she figures things out herself? But honestly the most important thing is to be non-judgemental and try to understand what's going on in her world. EDs can be super confusing to people who haven't experienced them, we get that.

So basic do's and don'ts that would apply to most people:Do ask questions and try to understand what's going on for her, every ED is different.Do try to figure out of she wants you to help, and if so, what she thinks would help.Don't do the above over meals (try to chose a more neutral time), and try to avoid making a big deal during mealtimes in general. Often the most helpful thing at those times is just having someone acting normal, it's a great distraction. If you're openly fixating on what/how she's eating then it ends up as a double whammy of anxiety. Obviously if she's openly super distressed or brings up the conversation herself it's different, but use your judgement.

since eating disorders have such a high fatality rate (1 in 5 die) a lot of medical professionals would rather escape liability and refuse to help/treat you. but i got good news for you, friend: you have the strength within you to recover. i am sure of it.

i have been struggling with anorexia and ARFID for three decades. therapy didn’t even work for me. all i was offered in terms of treatment were scammy inpatient services, where I KNEW I would starve even more. i was refused by a dozen nutritionists, psychiatrists, and therapists. no one wanted to risk treating me, basically, because I had a laundry list of comorbid mental health disorders.

fast forward to today: after overshooting my recovery weight by a tad, I am now stable at a very healthy weight for the first time in my life. but numbers don’t mean much, to be honest with you. it’s how you feel that’s important. how strong you are. how much energy you got. how stable your mood is. how willing are you to live.

even though i am mostly recovered, ED thoughts are still there, but I fight them every day. I know you can, too.

The first step to recovery in your situation is recognizing/acknowledging that there is a problem that needs fixing. Congratulations. You’ve done that. That’s no easy task, so I commend you for seeking help.

What broke the cycle for me was the realization that eating is not optional. You either eat, or you die. Anorexia has 20% fatality rate. It is an ugly, insidious disease that takes over your life and your relationships. It causes hair loss, osteoporosis, and sometimes irreparable or long-term organ damage, among a myriad of other things. The voice in your head that pleads with you to ignore the hunger signals, to skip this meal, and then the next, that voice is not your friend. You have to make a conscious effort to refuse this sort of self harm. I know it’s not easy. I know loving yourself is the hardest thing to do. But you deserve it. We all do.

Now, there are a few practical suggestions that I can make as part of a recovery plan (these are very subjective, just things that worked for me):

•	⁠journaling (writing helps me reason with the unhealthy urges my brain comes up with, sometimes.)

•	⁠not counting calories (look, even when my aim was to “get better,” counting calories ALWAYS resulted in me restricting my intake. Without fail.) I think, for most people with ED in the early stages of their recovery, counting calories is not beneficial. You could possibly keep a rudimentary meal log or something (while avoiding numbers) but I still wouldn’t recommend it.

•	⁠avoiding the scale and making a conscious effort to either 1. avoid mirrors or 2. retraining your brain by correcting your inner voice when you notice it being overly critical towards yourself. This is easier said than done, I know.

•	⁠you could benefit from the Science of Games (see the book SuperBetter by Jane McGonigal for more info) by turning your recovery into a game of sorts. Every meal is a power-up. They make you stronger to battle the Bad Guys (the personal challenges you face daily.) You’re the hero of your own story and your mission is to go for an Epic Win. You get it.

•	⁠make a list of Emergency Foods. For me, food repulsion was a huge part of my ED. I could not force myself to eat, otherwise I’d just throw up. So, what you can do is make a list of foods you can eat on Very Bad Days. For me, these were melons, most fruits, yogurt, oatmeal, rice, things like that. On bad days, rely on these. Shoot for at least two meals a day, mandatory. Even if they’re small meals (girl dinner, lol.) Count every small meal as a victory and celebrate it.

•	⁠reframe your thinking in terms of your relationship with food. Have you ever seen the cute anime Cells At Work? It’s like the cells in the human body, anthropomorphized. So think of each little cell in your body as cute little anime characters. Think of how much stronger, healthier, and happier you are making all these little anime cuties by nourishing them with food and water. Each time you eat and drink, they’re shouting with joy and singing and partying! I know it’s silly, but hey, this helped me, haha!

I wish you the best. Don’t forget, your journey is yours; not everything I’ve mentioned in here will apply to you. Find what works for you and don’t doubt the strength you have within. You got this!

text:
I’m 3 years recovered. But my ED is far less stereotypical, but maybe it could help putting my story here in case you can relate or anyone else. 
My ED was never fueled by body image, wanting to be thinner, or weight, or even food. 
After a bad breakup, and going no contact with my mother, my life suddenly went silent. Like all the chaos, abuse and drama I had been through just suddenly stopped all at once. My mother was an addict and had ED my entire life. I was guided into that sort of mindset from a young age, of always being hyper conscious of what I eat and how much. I spent years in constant mental and emotional distress. When I cut both my ex bf and mother out of my life, I realized my entire being was about survival and not about living. 
As I was hyper fixated on building a new life for myself, I just kind of forgot about fueling my body. Often found myself skipping breakfast and lunch, and when my roommates would get dinner I just didn’t have any interest at all. 
There wasn’t this mental gymnastics like traditional ED, I just simply wasn’t hungry for a long time. Once it became noticeable, I started to try to create a schedule for eating. But every single time I’d sit down to eat, I just couldn’t. I had no appetite and interest in food. I survived off of coffee and bagels for almost a year. 
Every single day, I’d meal prep and then throw away the food. Like the idea of sitting down to eat when I could be doing something else made my stomach tie in knots. 
Eventually I was out into an out patient program by my therapist. Which did me no good, because they were teaching me how to build a healthy relationship with food and I already had that established. 
I spent about 3 months visiting these therapy sessions and group sessions and never truly got nah better because they weren’t catering to my actual disorder. 
Food was just a mental block for me. I got to a point of wanting to eat so bad, and trying to buy special food to spike my interest. But after about 2 years nothing was working and I was wasting away. 
Finally I met with a childhood trauma therapist. We didn’t speak about food for the entire first year. But I didn’t notice over that year of working through my childhood trauma, my appetite was slowly coming back. 
I really appreciate my therapist for not stereotyping eating disorders, and categorizing me or putting me in a box. Previous therapists simply didn’t believe me, or didn’t even try to understand what was going on. They said I was unwilling to discuss my ED, when in reality ED was just a symptom of other mental health issues I was having. 
Because I was super into the gym, and a girl they just assumed I was unwilling to open up. I got kicked out of 2 programs for “lack of participation”. 
But keep pushing forward and looking for the right doctors for you. 
I found my doctor when my younger brother was diagnosed with ED. He was having the exact same issues as me. Our ED’s weren’t about the food, or weight, or body image. It ran much deeper, they weren’t driven by thoughts or emotions. 
I finally healed when I moved in with my bf and dad, and we were all in therapy. I realized creating a stable life with people I could trust was really the key to overcoming my mental health. It still took about a year for my body to truly let its guard down, and trust that I was safe again. 
But it’s almost like subconsciously, my body was rejecting life itself because it couldn’t trust that it was safe enough to live. Subconsciously I was shutting my body down, but unable to understand why I just couldn’t eat. If I tried forcing it, I’d gag through the entire meal, and feel sick to my stomach for days after. But my therapist told me to accept small meals in the mean time and stop pressuring myself to eat “normal”. 
This sort of ED is more common in children coming from severe abuse scenarios, women coming out of domestic violence, and men struggling with PTSD.
But I share my story, given the opportunity, in case it helps someone else out there struggling to find help

text:
From my experience it's addiction in that it's a misplaced coping mechanism. Addicts often struggle with some kind of trauma or abusive self talk that drives them to punish themselves or escape reality. Eating disorders can operate in a similar fashion. Repetitively punishing yourself because you believe you deserve it, controlling food as a means of ignoring underlying trauma or mental illness. 

The other aspect that ties it completely to addiction are the reward chemicals one can experience with certain behaviors. A relief of guilt by purging. A relief from emotional distress with the serotonin of eating endlessly. A relief of control issues by superceding your own bodies needs by your own twisted interpretation of 'willpower'. Often times even the feeling of emptiness or lightheadedness can give a sort of buzz. 

It doesn't help that the prevalence of diet culture conditions us to take pride and joy in restriction, and scales going down. It's ingrained in many societies that thinness is associated with many other positive traits. You may also recieve outside encouragement because people believe all weight loss is good.

 Emotional eating and binge eating are no exception. It is deeply held in many families and in our social culture of food that it is a reward or a soother of negative feelings. Ice cream after a breakup, dessert stomach, "clean your plate". Many adults don't realize that pushing a child to eat past their comfort can throw off their fullness and hunger cues, and their relationship with food. It's like becoming an alcoholic because your father always drank. 

Eating disorders follow the same patterns of escapism that addictions do. Targeted therapy and recovery are important to heal past both!

This is really tricky. Obviously everyone is different, but I know that for a lot of people, eating disorders are really really hard to talk and open up about, because people struggle to understand. I always worry that people are judging me, think I’m pathetic, making issues out of nothing, should ‘get over it’, ‘just eat’, there’s ‘nothing wrong with you...’ While your comment may have just been ignorance, in her eyes it could’ve indicated more such as a lack of sympathy towards her. The fact that she’s previously opened up to you is a really good sign. That you betrayed that trust, is not. But, it’s very easy to slip up accidentally and not realise that what you’re saying can hurt someone you love, especially when it’s hard to understand their disorder. I trust that the fact that you’re seeking advice, realise your mistake and want to fix it is a good indication that what you said was completely unintentional and accidental. 

My partner is not educated on eating disorders. He admits to not knowing much or understanding. But he tries his best to be deeply emphatic and sympathetic. I think the best thing you can do is listen to her. Encourage her to open up more about how she’s feeling, her past, her present, her thoughts. Then show, again and again, that she CAN in fact trust you with what she tells you. This will take time. She won’t open up all in one go, especially considering you’ve recently broken her trust. But proving that it was a genuine mistake can only be done by showing that you won’t do it again. 

Perhaps research more into her disorder in your own time. You don’t necessarily need to tell her you’ve done this, but it may help give you an insight into how she’s feeling before she tells you. This gives you a chance to prepare yourself - what to say, what definitely not to say. Yet, the most important thing is to actively listen to her. Never be dismissive of her, particularly when she’s opening up.

This is all I can think of to help with long term healing, but this is not a quick fix. In the meantime, there’s slightly more stereotypical, less meaningful things you can do to show that you’re sorry and that you love her. These are still important for short term forgiveness - you can say you’re sorry all you want, but these help show that you are as you’re putting thought and action into the apology. Flowers, a handwritten letter (possibly apology letter), plan date night, other stuff more attuned to your relationship. 

Overall, communication is key to solving this. Sit down with her, and perhaps even ask if there’s anything she specifically needs from you to help you both move past this.

When I judge other people’s bodies, I then try to ask my self “so?” To which I used to reply “but it’s not healthy it’s so bad to be overweight!” However, it is really hard to tell what “healthy” is. I used to point to BMI (ok I still do it’s a process alright) but really that doesn’t reflect health. There are other tests/calculations that try to measure body health with a number but, really, how silly is that? Being healthy is so complex, any evaluation resulting in  one number could never really reflect what is going on. 

Now, to be completely honest when I was inwardly shaming people about their body, was I really concerned? Probably not. That was some bull shit fact that “aligned” with what I wanted so I could smugly think “I’m right, they’re wrong.” If I truly valued their well being, I should try to be kind and understanding. Also, aren’t there other factors, like sleep, that significantly contribute to health that I was just completely ignoring? I would never shame someone for not getting 8 hours every night, in fact I don’t really care how much sleep other people get at night. 

So ya, I mean we already know that “fat” is really a societal stigma, perhaps cloaked with the ideas of good intentions and health but really is kinda illogical (ugh do I sound like a rationalist kill me now if yes promise I am not hopefully). However, what if I never had any pretenses about health? I mean, how does the above change my preferences for what I think the/a human body should look like? And to that I say: I have no idea. 

But! since having that realization (ok and tbh having it time and time again when I forget), it is easier for me to see other body types as good and beautiful. (Oh and looking at ancient statues - aw shit finding answers in the classics? I swear I’m not a rationalist). I find that when I am less judgmental about other people I tend to be less judge mental about myself. 

Whew alright see I’m not saying “it’s not logical so don’t believe it! Logic will get you through life!” Because that is a load of barnacles, really what helps is the *continual* emotional realization that my “good intentions” were in fact the opposite, and people can figure out their shit on their own, and tbh I should be focusing on myself before I try to smugly hide behind a scale. 

Don’t get me wrong, I still Fuck Up like, all the time and also I realize that I didn’t really give a good tip on how to do the accepting, I just pointed out why I try to accept which is a step you’re already trying to make. Ugh. Oh well,

Idk if this will help you, but I don’t take the whole pack with me to the living room/table/wherever I’m eating.
